checkpoints: Risk 1 — the access key/secret key is a long-lived credential that never expires until manually deleted, so if the Secret is exposed (loose RBAC, an accidental log print, a leaked etcd backup), an attacker gets permanent AWS access without anyone knowing.

Risk 2 — the same key is shared by every Pod referencing that Secret, so CloudTrail logs only show "IAM user X called it," not which specific Pod made the call, losing per-workload audit/traceability.
Risk 3 — rotating the key requires generating a new key, editing the Secret, and restarting every Pod that used the old key, a manual step that's easy to forget and disruptive.

IRSA mechanism (token issuance) — via the Pod's annotated ServiceAccount, it receives a short-lived OIDC token signed by the cluster itself (expiring in about an hour by default, auto-rotated by the kubelet).
IRSA mechanism (assume role) — the AWS SDK inside the Pod uses that token to call sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.

IRSA mechanism (verify + issue) — AWS STS verifies the signature via the registered OIDC provider, checks the sub/aud conditions, and issues a temporary credential scoped to the role's exact permissions.

This resolves all three risks at once: no static AWS key ever exists in the cluster to leak (risk 1), each ServiceAccount maps to its own identity so CloudTrail can pin down exactly which Pod called (risk 2), and the token auto-rotates by design so nobody manually rotates keys or restarts Pods (risk 3).
Root cause is not hardware — kubectl top node already shows the node has spare CPU/RAM, ruling out a resource/hardware fault.

VPC CNI works differently from overlay CNIs (Calico/Flannel, which assign virtual IPs in a private overlay network): it assigns each Pod a real IP that lives inside the VPC subnet itself, via Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs) attached to the EC2 instance.
This design lets Pods talk natively to other AWS resources (e.g. RDS, ALB) without NAT.
This design also lets security groups apply all the way down to the Pod level.

The trade-off is that each EC2 instance type supports a fixed number of ENIs and a fixed number of IPs per ENI (a t3.medium gets only about 17 IPs available for Pods) — once that budget is used up, a new Pod cannot get an IP assigned no matter how much spare CPU/RAM the node has; this is IP exhaustion, a limit entirely independent of compute resources.

Fix 1: enable prefix delegation (ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true) on the VPC CNI add-on so each ENI gets a /28 prefix (16 contiguous IPs) instead of individual IPs, substantially raising the Pods-per-node ceiling without adding ENIs or changing the subnet.
Fix 2: switch the node to a larger instance type that has more ENIs and IPs per AWS's limits table.
Both fixes target the real root cause (available IPs for Pods), unlike restarting the node or suspecting a hardware fault, which don't address the actual problem.
Fargate cannot run a DaemonSet — every Pod on Fargate is its own isolated micro-VM with no concept of a shared node for a DaemonSet Pod to attach to.

Because of that, the existing log-shipper DaemonSet has nowhere to live on an all-Fargate architecture and would need a redesign (e.g. a sidecar container in every Pod instead of one shared DaemonSet).
Fargate bills exactly by the vCPU/RAM each Pod requests, a model that fits bursty/batch workloads needing high isolation (e.g. CI runners, batch jobs) — not workloads with steady, continuous load.

For the web Deployments running steady, continuous load, an optimized Managed Node Group (Reserved Instances/Savings Plans, bin-packing many small Pods onto fewer larger nodes) is almost always cheaper than paying Fargate per individual Pod.
Managed Node Group lets AWS handle the EC2 lifecycle (provisioning, draining during AMI updates, Auto Scaling Group) — the best balance of control and convenience, and the sensible default.
Self-managed Node Group offers maximum flexibility (custom AMIs, exotic GPUs) but you own every operational concern — only pick it when managed can't meet a special need.

The sensible architecture: keep the log-shipper agent and the steady-load web Deployments on a Managed Node Group, and move only the genuinely bursty/batch workloads (no DaemonSet dependency) to a separate Fargate profile scoped by namespace or label selector — mixing two data planes in one cluster, each serving what it's actually good at.

Root cause is an IAM/IRSA bug, not a storage bug — the csi-provisioner log shows an authorization error (`is not authorized to perform: ec2:CreateVolume because no identity-based policy allows the ec2:CreateVolume action`).

If the real cause were a wrong StorageClass or AZ capacity exhaustion, the log would show a different kind of error (e.g. `InvalidParameterValue`, `no available zones`) rather than a clear authorization message — so the error type itself rules out the storage explanation.
Second piece of evidence: `kubectl get sa ebs-csi-controller-sa -n kube-system` shows empty annotations — the ServiceAccount is missing the `eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn` annotation.

That missing annotation is the IRSA wiring: without it the EKS Pod Identity Webhook never injects `AWS_ROLE_ARN` plus a projected OIDC token into the controller pod, so the AWS SDK inside it has no credentials at all to call the EC2 API — it's not a wrong-permission role, it's no role at all.
Consequence: the PVC hangs at `Pending` forever at the Provisioning step because the controller never actually manages to create the volume, not because of missing capacity or a wrong StorageClass.

Fix step 1: reattach the correct `eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn=<ARN of the IRSA role for EBS CSI>` annotation to the `ebs-csi-controller-sa` ServiceAccount via Terraform, not a one-off manual `kubectl annotate`, so the fix isn't lost on the next apply.
Fix step 2: run `kubectl rollout restart deployment ebs-csi-controller -n kube-system` so a new controller pod actually picks up the IRSA token.
Verification: the PVC turns `Bound` within a few seconds and the csi-provisioner log no longer shows any `is not authorized` lines.

Uses `principals { type = "Federated", identifiers = [aws_iam_openid_connect_provider.eks.arn] }` — trusts the cluster's OIDC provider as a federated external identity, not an AWS service principal (`Service`).
Uses `actions = ["sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity"]` — the action specific to OIDC/web-identity federation, distinct from `sts:AssumeRole`.
Includes a `sub` condition (`test = "StringEquals"`) pinned to the exact value `system:serviceaccount:default:s3-reader`, restricting trust to only that ServiceAccount in that namespace.

Includes a mandatory `aud` condition (`test = "StringEquals"`) pinned to `sts.amazonaws.com`, preventing tokens issued for a different audience from being usable to assume the role even if `sub` matches.

Both the `sub` and `aud` condition variable keys are built the same way — stripping the `https://` scheme from the OIDC provider's issuer URL (e.g. `"${replace(aws_iam_openid_connect_provider.eks.url, "https://", "")}:sub"` / `:aud`) — the required key format for a Federated-OIDC condition.
The `aws_iam_role.irsa` resource sets `assume_role_policy = data.aws_iam_policy_document.irsa_trust.json`, actually attaching this trust policy document to the IAM role.

Xác định vấn đề 1 — thiếu IRSA wiring: code tạo đúng aws_iam_role.alb_controller và attach policy, nhưng KHÔNG có kubernetes_service_account resource set annotation eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn trỏ vào role đó, và helm_release cũng không có set { name = "serviceAccount.create" value = "false" }.

Hậu quả của vấn đề 1: vì thiếu wiring, chart fallback về serviceAccount.create = true mặc định nên Helm tự tạo một ServiceAccount aws-load-balancer-controller MỚI không có annotation IRSA — trong khi IAM role dù tạo đúng nhưng không bao giờ được nối vào ServiceAccount đang chạy thật; hệ quả là controller Pod chạy dưới ServiceAccount không có quyền này không gọi được ELBv2 API (CreateLoadBalancer, RegisterTargets...), khiến MỌI Ingress/Service kiểu LoadBalancer trong cluster treo vĩnh viễn mà không bao giờ tạo ra LB thật — lỗi dễ bị bỏ sót vì nhìn qua tưởng IAM setup "đã đúng" (cả role và policy đều tồn tại) nhưng hai nửa chưa được nối với nhau.

Fix cho vấn đề 1: thêm resource kubernetes_service_account với annotation eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn = aws_iam_role.alb_controller.arn, đồng thời thêm set { name = "serviceAccount.create" value = "false" } trong helm_release để chart tái sử dụng ServiceAccount đã annotate thay vì tạo mới.
Xác định vấn đề 2 — không kiểm soát thứ tự teardown: không có gì đảm bảo các Ingress/Service kiểu LoadBalancer bị xoá TRƯỚC khi helm_release (controller) bị terraform destroy gỡ bỏ.

Hậu quả của vấn đề 2: nếu controller bị gỡ trước, các ALB/NLB mà nó đã tạo trở thành orphaned resource — không còn controller theo dõi để dọn dẹp, cũng không nằm trong Terraform state (vì được tạo qua API call của controller chứ không phải Terraform resource) — kết quả là bị tính phí vô thời hạn cho đến khi ai đó phát hiện và tự xoá thủ công qua Console.

Fix cho vấn đề 2: đưa vào runbook vận hành bước bắt buộc kubectl delete svc,ingress --all (hoặc giới hạn theo namespace liên quan) và chờ controller thực sự xoá các LB thật TRƯỚC KHI chạy terraform destroy trên helm_release; nếu cần enforce bằng code thì cân nhắc bước verify thủ công hoặc wrapper script quanh terraform destroy thay vì trông chờ vào việc ai đó nhớ đúng thứ tự.

Root risk: applying `authentication_mode = "API"` in a single-step `apply` is a self-lockout trap — the moment it takes effect, EKS stops reading the `aws-auth` ConfigMap for authorization entirely, so if no access entries exist yet, nobody (including whoever just ran the apply) can `kubectl` into the cluster anymore.

Step 1: before touching `authentication_mode`, create an `aws_eks_access_entry` (with an `aws_eks_access_policy_association` attaching the right policy, e.g. `AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy`) for every admin IAM principal while the mode is still `CONFIG_MAP` — safe because the ConfigMap is still the active authorization mechanism at this point.

Step 2: switch `authentication_mode` to `API_AND_CONFIG_MAP` as a transition state, where both the old ConfigMap and the new access entries authorize in parallel, so the ConfigMap acts as a fallback safety net if Step 1's access entries have a mistake (missing principal, wrong policy).

Step 3: run mandatory verification via `kubectl auth can-i --list --as=<ARN>` for every admin principal to confirm each one already has access purely through an access entry, fully independent of the ConfigMap.
Only after that verification passes 100% do you apply one final time to switch `authentication_mode` all the way to `API`, cutting off the old ConfigMap authorization path for good.

The value of splitting into these three steps (access entries first -> parallel transition mode -> verify then cut over) is that the migration stays safely rollback-able at every stage, and the cluster is never left in a state where nobody has access.
A `git push` is recognized by GitHub as an event, and a matching trigger (`on: push`) declared in a workflow YAML file under `.github/workflows/` kicks off that workflow.
A workflow contains one or more jobs, and each job is scheduled to run on its own separate runner — a fresh VM (usually `ubuntu-latest`) freshly provisioned by GitHub for that job.

Each job runs a sequence of steps in order; a step is either `run:` (a shell command executed directly on the runner) or `uses:` (calling a reusable action — from the GitHub Marketplace like `actions/checkout@v4`, or a custom one).
`GITHUB_TOKEN` is automatically generated and injected by GitHub into every job, scoped exactly to the repo and job that's running, so nobody has to manually create or store a Personal Access Token.
The workflow must explicitly declare `permissions: packages: write`, since the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` doesn't have write access to packages.

Building and pushing the Docker image is done via the `docker/build-push-action` action, which authenticates using the auto-injected `GITHUB_TOKEN` to log into and push to `ghcr.io/<owner>/<repo>:<tag>` — completing the chain trigger → workflow → job → runner → step → action → GITHUB_TOKEN → GHCR that produces the green checkmark.
Explains that `@v4` (or `@main`) is a mutable Git tag — merely a pointer to a commit — and that pointer can be moved to point at a different commit at any time.

Notes the move can be made either by the action's legitimate maintainer releasing a new version, or by an attacker who gained push access (compromised account or a merged malicious PR) — in either case without your team knowing.
Explains that GitHub Actions resolves `@v4` to whatever commit the tag currently points to at the exact moment the workflow runs, not the commit that existed when the pipeline was set up.

States the resulting blast radius: if the tag has been moved to malicious code, the runner automatically executes it with full access to secrets, the repo's source code, and anything else the runner can reach.
Notes that this is exactly the kind of supply-chain attack that has happened in the wild (not just a theoretical risk).

Explains that pinning to a full SHA fixes the root cause because a SHA is immutable — a cryptographic hash of the exact content at one specific commit — so it can never be made to point at different content (any change produces a different SHA).
States that SHA pinning guarantees the workflow always runs exactly the code the team reviewed and accepted once, no matter what happens to the tag afterward.

Mentions the practical mitigation for the maintenance burden of SHA pinning: use Dependabot (or an equivalent tool) to automatically open a PR bumping to the new SHA whenever a new release comes out, so updates are still reviewed but without manually looking up SHAs by hand.
Root cause: this is not a code bug — the required `security-scan` status check has never actually run for this PR (it wasn't triggered and failed; it was simply never scheduled).

Mechanism: the workflow containing `security-scan` most likely has a `paths:` filter in its `on:` block (e.g. only triggering on `.ts`/`.go`/`Dockerfile` changes) that a PR touching only `README.md` doesn't match, so the workflow never fires for this PR.

Why the UI shows "Expected — Waiting for status to be reported": branch protection with a required status check waits for that check to report at least one result (success or failure) before allowing merge; since the workflow never runs, no result is ever reported.
Consequence: the pending state persists indefinitely — the PR is not automatically rejected by branch protection, it simply never becomes eligible to merge.
Fix option 1: broaden the `security-scan` workflow's `paths:` filter to include non-code changes, or drop the filter entirely for this job (accepting it then runs on every PR).

Fix option 2 (more durable): add a job that always runs regardless of the `paths:` filter, checks the relevant condition itself, and reports "skipped → success" when the change is outside the scan's scope — guaranteeing the required check always reports a concrete result to branch protection no matter what the PR touches.
